overview: Austronesian names a language family and many peoples, not one kingdom or uniform culture. The atlas shows 4000 to 323 BCE, with broad shapes across western Indonesia and sometimes the Philippines. These are not reliable migration fronts: they omit Taiwan and the Pacific, and their earliest spread is too broad to treat as established history. Examples here distinguish particular places, periods and later traditions.

periods.title: An early atlas label, not a founding date
periods.summary: This opening interval is map coverage; it does not establish that all highlighted islands already spoke related languages.

periods.title: Voyages and encounters in Island Southeast Asia
periods.summary: Research places major dispersals from Taiwan roughly within this broad period; newcomers encountered societies with much older local histories.

periods.title: Pacific settlement and expanding exchange
periods.summary: Lapita communities reached Remote Oceania during this interval, beyond the atlas shapes; island societies continued changing after its endpoint.

items.text: Related languages eventually connected communities from Madagascar to Rapa Nui, but people formed very different societies. A language family is a historical relationship between languages, not a test of someone’s appearance, ancestry or citizenship.

A widely supported model places a major movement from Taiwan into Island Southeast Asia about 4,000 to 4,500 years ago. Wallacea, including Sulawesi and the islands farther east, already had inhabitants with histories stretching back tens of thousands of years. Migration brought encounters and exchange, not a discovery of universally empty land.

A 2022 study of ancient DNA from 16 people in Wallacea found different histories in northern and southern islands, with repeated population mixing. Its samples span roughly the last 2,600 years, mostly later than this map. The result cautions against a single arrow representing every voyage, family or language change.

sections.title: Food, cloth and places to live

items.text: At Nagsabaran in northern Luzon, a small excavation trench produced 79 rice grains or fragments and 224 examples of Job’s tears, another edible cereal, in its Neolithic layer. These tiny charred remains turn “farming” into identifiable crops. The regional Neolithic began roughly 4,200 to 4,000 years ago, among people already living in the Cagayan valley.

Nagsabaran’s Neolithic finds also include clay spindle whorls, polished stone adzes and a jade bracelet fragment. Whorls helped a spindle turn while fibers became thread; adzes shaped wood. The assemblage joins food production, making useful things and personal adornment in the same community.

At Peinan in eastern Taiwan, excavation plans and museum reconstructions show dwellings oriented toward the Taitung plain, away from the mountains. Finds include tools for farming, fishing, hunting, carpentry, weaving and food preparation. These homes belonged to a particular archaeological community; they are not a universal Austronesian house plan.

Peinan’s late Neolithic jade use peaked roughly 3,500 to 2,500 years ago. More than 5,000 jade objects have been excavated, mostly as offerings in slate coffins. Yet there is little jade-working waste. Researchers therefore suspect many finished pieces arrived from specialist workshops near Taiwan’s Fengtian jade source.

The Peinan cemetery contains more than 2,000 slate coffins. Carefully made jade and pottery accompanied some burials. These are records of how communities treated the dead across generations, as well as valuable objects; the richness of a burial cannot tell us every detail of the person’s household.

sections.title: A stone can travel farther than its maker

items.text: A jade bracelet from Nagsabaran, dated about 1800 to 1500 BCE, was traced to Fengtian nephrite in eastern Taiwan. Its size resembles older Taiwanese bracelets. The stone gives evidence of a sea connection even when no ship survives. It does not reveal whether the wearer, trader or craftsperson spoke a particular language.

From around 500 BCE, near this map’s end, jade exchange expanded widely around the South China Sea and continued for centuries afterward. Unfinished ornaments and offcuts show manufacture in several places. At Khao Sam Kaeo in Thailand, an older Taiwanese jade adze was being reshaped into a pendant: a stone tool could enjoy a second career as jewelry.

sections.title: Pacific communities beyond the highlighted islands

items.text: Lapita is an archaeological label for a distinctive Pacific material tradition, not a synonym for every Austronesian-speaking society. Its potters combined small toothed-stamp impressions into elaborate geometric patterns, sometimes including faces. The name comes from a site in New Caledonia, far outside this atlas record’s shapes.
At Teouma in Vanuatu, bones of 49 adults buried around 3,000 years ago indicate protein from reef foods, domestic animals and fruit bats. Their diets combined sea and land resources.

Later movements into Vanuatu brought substantial new ancestry from Near Oceania while Austronesian languages continued. Researchers compared ancient DNA with linguistic history to identify this contrast. Languages can survive major demographic changes; a community’s speech and its family tree do not have to follow identical paths.

A much later Amis example shows why boats were also working places. Taiwan’s National Museum of Prehistory describes an 1803 castaway account of bamboo craft used by two or three fishers, with woven bamboo sails and a rear platform for preparing food. A fishing trip needed room for lunch as well as the catch. This is not a reconstruction of a Neolithic voyage.

For a securely dated language sample, the 2026 Nanshi Amis learning list gives wawa, meaning “child.” These Roman letters are the modern written form used in that teaching resource. This is one living Austronesian language in Taiwan, not a surviving prehistoric inscription or a phrase spoken identically by all Austronesian peoples.

Modern language learning also uses songs, picture books and games. An Indigenous Languages Research and Development Foundation report covering resources in 2024 describes touch games, audiobooks, animations and classroom videos. This is present-day educational work helping children and other learners use their languages, not evidence of ancient schools.

ending.text: The atlas stops in 323 BCE, but Austronesian-speaking communities did not disappear. Their languages and institutions kept changing through distinct island histories, later kingdoms, colonial encounters and modern states. There is no single fall, ruler or successor for this language family.
